title: 9 Christmas Kitchen Decorations That Look EXPENSIVE (Mostly Free)

scenes.text: Sweetheart, everybody decorates the living room for Christmas. The tree, the mantel, the front door. And then they forget the one room where the whole family actually spends Christmas. The kitchen. That's where the cookies get baked, where the coffee gets poured, where the aunts sit and talk until midnight. My mother always said, the kitchen is the heart of Christmas, so it should look like it.
scenes.caption: THE HEART OF CHRISTMAS

scenes.text: So tonight I'm giving you nine ways to make your kitchen feel like Christmas, most of them free, without cluttering up the counters you need for cooking. And stay with me, because the last one isn't something you see at all. It's something you smell, and it makes the whole house feel like Christmas the minute people walk in the door.
scenes.caption: NINE KITCHEN IDEAS

scenes.text: Our kitchen on Elm Street was small, yellow, with a white enamel stove and a window over the sink that looked out on the backyard. Every December, my mother turned it into the coziest room in Ohio, with almost nothing. A few branches, some red ribbon, a bowl of oranges, and her good tablecloth. And the smell of something always baking.
scenes.caption: THE COZIEST ROOM IN OHIO

scenes.text: She had one rule. Nothing on the counters that gets in the way of the cooking. A kitchen has to work at Christmas harder than any other time of the year. So she decorated up high, on the walls, the windows and the tops of cabinets, and left the counters clear. In a minute I'll show you how, starting with the window over the sink.
scenes.caption: NOTHING IN THE WAY

scenes.text: Number one. The window over the sink, because that's where you spend the most time looking. Hang a small wreath in the window on a ribbon. Or lay a little garland of cedar along the sill, with a few pinecones. Or hang a row of three dried orange slices, or paper snowflakes, on thin thread. My mother hung a little red bell that rang when she opened the window.
scenes.caption: WHERE YOU LOOK MOST

scenes.text: And put a small potted plant on the windowsill. A little rosemary plant trimmed like a Christmas tree, or a paperwhite bulb, or a Christmas cactus. Rosemary is my favorite, honey, because it looks like a tiny tree and you can snip it for the turkey. Mine is eleven years old now. Every December, I tie a little red bow on it.
scenes.caption: A TINY TREE

scenes.text: Number two. The tops of the cabinets. That's the most wasted space in the whole kitchen. Lay a long garland of greenery across the tops, with a string of warm battery lights tucked in. It makes the whole room glow at night, and it's completely out of the way. My granddaughter does this every year, and she says it's the only decoration the cat can't reach.
scenes.query: garland on top of kitchen cabinets
scenes.caption: THE CAT CAN'T REACH IT

scenes.text: Number three. If you have an open shelf, or a hutch, swap a few everyday things for Christmas ones. Put out the red and white dishes, a few old cookie tins, a jar of candy canes, a stack of Christmas mugs. Mix in a few sprigs of greenery. You're not adding clutter, honey. You're just trading what's already there for something more festive.
scenes.caption: TRADE, DON'T ADD

scenes.text: And if you have any old Christmas dishes from your mother or grandmother, this is the time to use them. Don't keep them in a box. My mother's Christmas plates are white with a little holly border, from Woolworth's in nineteen fifty-five. They cost a dollar each. I eat breakfast off them every day in December, and every time, I think of her.
scenes.caption: USE THE OLD DISHES

scenes.text: Number four, and this is the easiest one. Change the towels and the linens. A red and white checked dish towel, a plaid oven mitt, a Christmas tablecloth on the kitchen table. That's all it takes, and it changes the whole feeling of the room in five minutes. And it costs almost nothing if you buy them the week after Christmas, for next year.
scenes.caption: FIVE MINUTES

scenes.text: If this is helping you, honey, tap the like button for me. It helps Grandma more than you know. And put a small rug in front of the sink, in red or plaid. It's soft on your feet when you're standing there doing dishes for the fourteenth time on Christmas Day. In my family, the dishes take longer than the dinner.
scenes.caption: THE FOURTEENTH TIME

scenes.text: Number five. The kitchen table, the one where the family eats breakfast. Keep it simple, so you can still use it. A small bowl of clementines with a few sprigs of greenery. Or a pitcher of evergreen branches with a red bow. Or a little row of three candles on a tray. Something you can lift off in one move when it's time to roll out the cookie dough.
scenes.caption: ONE MOVE

scenes.text: So far, the window over the sink, the tops of the cabinets, the open shelf, the towels, and the kitchen table. And here's a tip about that bowl of clementines, honey. They're food and decoration at the same time. My mother put a bowl of oranges on the table all December, and we were allowed to take one any time we wanted. In the fifties, an orange in December felt like a present.
scenes.caption: LIKE A PRESENT

scenes.text: And hang a few things on the cabinet doors, honey. A small wreath on a ribbon over the door of the cabinet with the glasses, or a sprig of mistletoe tied with red string to the knob of the kitchen door. My mother hung mistletoe there every year, and my father would stand under it, waiting, with his coffee cup, until she noticed him. She always pretended not to see him for a good long while.
scenes.query: small wreath on kitchen cabinet door
scenes.caption: UNDER THE MISTLETOE

scenes.text: Number six. The refrigerator door. That's where the family's whole life goes in December. Clear off the old magnets and papers, and hang the Christmas cards there as they come in, or the children's drawings, or the family photo. My mother tied a red ribbon around the refrigerator handle, like a present. My father said it was the only present in the house he could open every day.
scenes.caption: OPEN IT EVERY DAY

scenes.text: Number seven. Bring out something old. A vintage cookie jar. An old rolling pin with a ribbon tied on it, hung on the wall. Your grandmother's tin cookie cutters on a hook. A handwritten recipe card in a little frame. Old kitchen things have a warmth that nothing new can buy. And they start conversations. Every child who comes in my kitchen asks about Grandma Pearl's rolling pin.
scenes.query: vintage rolling pin cookie cutters wall
scenes.caption: SOMETHING OLD

scenes.text: Number eight. Soft light at night. After supper, turn off the bright overhead light in the kitchen, and leave on only the little light over the stove, the lights on top of the cabinets, and a candle on the table. That's when the kitchen feels the coziest. The whole family drifts in for cocoa and cookies, and nobody wants to leave.
scenes.query: kitchen at night soft light candle
scenes.caption: NOBODY WANTS TO LEAVE

scenes.text: And now number nine, the one I promised you, the one you don't see at all. The smell. Put a small pot of water on the stove on very low heat. Add a few orange peels, a cinnamon stick, five or six whole cloves, a slice of fresh ginger, and a sprig of pine or rosemary. Let it simmer gently all afternoon, adding water as it goes down.
scenes.caption: THE SMELL OF CHRISTMAS

scenes.text: In half an hour, the whole house smells like Christmas, honey. Like oranges and spice and pine. Better than any candle you can buy. People walk in the front door and say, oh, what are you baking? And you can say, nothing yet. Keep it on the back burner on low, and never leave it on when you leave the house or go to bed.
scenes.caption: WHAT ARE YOU BAKING?

scenes.text: And use your scraps, sweetheart. Save the peels from the clementines in a bag in the icebox, with the ends of the cinnamon sticks and the rosemary stems. Toss them in the pot. It costs nothing at all. My mother made hers with apple peels and cloves, and she said it kept the whole family in a good mood until New Year's.
scenes.caption: IT COSTS NOTHING

scenes.text: And make a little cocoa station, sweetheart, on one corner of the counter you don't cook on. A tray with a jar of cocoa mix, a jar of mini marshmallows, a jar of candy canes, and a few Christmas mugs hanging on hooks or stacked. It's a decoration and a treat at the same time. The grandchildren make their own all December, and the tray is always a happy mess.
scenes.caption: A COCOA STATION

scenes.text: And a word about keeping it all practical. Keep every decoration away from the stove, the toaster and anything hot. No paper or dried greens near the burners. Keep the counters clear for cooking. And put everything away by the sixth of January, so the kitchen goes back to work. A Christmas kitchen should be beautiful, but it should still make supper.
scenes.caption: IT SHOULD STILL MAKE SUPPER

scenes.text: So one more time. A wreath or greens in the window over the sink. A garland on top of the cabinets. Christmas dishes on the shelf. Red towels and a plaid rug. A bowl of oranges on the table. Cards on the refrigerator. Something old on the wall. Soft light at night. And a pot of orange peels and cinnamon simmering on the stove. That's the heart of Christmas.
scenes.caption: THE HEART OF CHRISTMAS

scenes.text: Tell me in the comments, sweetheart. What did your grandmother's kitchen smell like at Christmas? I'd love to know. The whole playlist of Grandma's Christmas tips is right there on your screen, and I'll see you in the next video. Good night, honey. Merry Christmas.
scenes.caption: WHAT DID IT SMELL LIKE?
